title: Awareness-Illumination Against the Stream
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Transcribed from A Treatise on the Noumenon of the Universe

inline.s: Transcribed from A Treatise on the Noumenon of the Universe

A Treatise on the Noumenon of the Universe is a monumental work of Buddhadharma that marks an epoch, bridging what came before with what follows — an outline of the teaching of a whole age, a torch for the chaotic times of the dharma's decline. Compiled by the white-robed layman Dingxi of Jinling from his wide reading of the scriptures, it may well be called ‘a new Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna.’”

The book takes as its title A Treatise on the Noumenon of the Universe because, since ancient times, philosophy East and West has striven tirelessly to seek out the noumenon of the universe. The book therefore proclaims to the world that Śākyamuni Buddha gave the correct answer more than two thousand years ago:
the noumenon of the universe is the true reality of all dharmas, and the universe is a dream born of ignorance — and it further shows how to awaken from that dream.
(See, for details,
The True Reality of All Dharmas
.) Looking at modern science, the Buddha's conclusions are being confirmed one by one, revealing ever more clearly the Buddha's great wisdom, ultimate and perfect.

Because the author of this book concealed his name, nothing is known of his life, and we can only come to know the man through his writing: he was a lay Buddhist of Jinling (Nanjing), a contemporary of Master Yinguang or perhaps a little later. His style name was Dingxi. Dingxi is a homophone of ding xi — ‘certainly reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.’ The gentleman was not only thorough and penetrating in the principles of Buddhadharma and learned in both Eastern and Western thought, but his own level of cultivation and realization was exceedingly high: thoroughly versed in both Chan and Pure Land, with boundless compassion. Truly he was a great bodhisattva.

[Awareness-Illumination Against the Stream] To turn back and look within. ‘Against the stream’: to follow sounds outward and chase after forms is to go with the stream; to turn hearing back and look inward is to go against the stream. The core practice of awareness-illumination against the stream in this piece is:
watching where thoughts arise.
Note:
The subheadings in the text were added by the annotator.

[The present single thought — its essence is the dharma-realm itself. Following defiled conditions, it runs loose and scatters, and the whole of the true becomes the false. Following the nature of enlightenment, one enters the stream and turns the light back, and the whole of the false is the true.]

The present single thought — its essence is the true mind. By following defiled conditions, it runs loose and disperses, and the whole of the true mind is transformed into the false mind (the whole of the true becomes the false). If instead one follows the nature of enlightenment, enters the stream, and turns the light back, then the whole of the false mind is transformed into the true mind (the whole of the false is the true).
[Dharma-realm] The term ‘dharma-realm’ has many meanings. Here it is another name for the true mind. Direct Explanation of the True Mind
Other Names for the True Mind says:

“Apart from delusion it is called true; its numinous mirroring is called mind. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra sets forth this mind. Someone asked, ‘Is it then merely called the true mind, or has it other names besides?’ The reply: ‘The teaching of the Buddha and the teaching of the patriarchs establish names differently.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra establishes it as the dharma-realm, because all things interpenetrate and mutually contain.’”

[Running loose and scattering] ‘Scattering’ means to be dispersed and lost. [Entering the stream] To follow sounds and chase forms is to flow outward; to turn hearing back and look inward is to enter the stream. The habitual tendencies of beginningless kalpas flow outward, and so rebirth goes on without end; now one reverses all this, enters the stream and looks within, returning to the root and the source.
[The whole of the true becomes the false, the whole of the false is the true]

The mind of the present single thought has two states, true and false: when the self-nature is master, it is true; when habit is master, it is false. ‘The whole of the true becomes the false, the whole of the false is the true’ means that the true and the false cannot both stand — it is either wholly true or wholly false. With one deluded thought, the whole of the true mind turns into the false mind (the whole of the true becomes the false); with one awakened thought, the whole of the false mind turns into the true mind (the whole of the false is the true). Here ‘true’ means the original state — the true mind is the mind's original state; ‘false’ is the false of deluded movement, that is, disorder. Because the original state is muddied and disordered by deluded movement, the true mind becomes the false mind. The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“A deluded thought before, and one is an ordinary being; an awakened thought after, and one is a Buddha.”

[If one understands the one nature and does not turn with consciousness, then there are no two marks, and all dharmas are just so. Whatever arises — the stirring of mind and movement of thought, deliberation and discrimination, seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing, walking, standing, sitting, lying, dressing, eating — all are the deluded functioning that arises from the noumenon, all are illusory shadows manifested by one's own mind.]

If one realizes that the true mind and the false mind are originally one in essence, and does not turn with consciousness, then there are no two marks of true and false, and all dharmas are originally just so. Whatever arises — the stirring of mind and movement of thought, deliberation and discrimination, seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing, walking, standing, sitting, lying, dressing, eating — all are the deluded functioning that arises from the noumenon (the self-nature), all are illusory shadows manifested by one's own mind.

[One nature] The true mind and the false mind are originally one in essence. From the Buddhas above to the wriggling and flying creatures below, though their kinds differ in a thousand ways, none is not rooted in the one nature. Deluded, it becomes birth and death; awakened, it becomes nirvāṇa. Though delusion and awakening differ, their essence is originally one — this is the one nature. [Wriggling and flying (
rú fěi
)] Wriggling and flying insects. [Deluded functioning] Absurd and unreasonable misuse. [All are illusory shadows manifested by one's own mind]
“Whatever has marks is unreal.”
(The Diamond Sūtra)

[One who can know that body and mind are the delusion of ignorance, like flowers in the sky with no nature of their own, dreamlike and unreal, should turn away from all illusory and false transformations, dissolve the existent back into emptiness, trace back to the root and exhaust the source: the ten thousand dharmas are one substance, all returning to the true and pure.]

When one can know that body and mind are deluded appearances of ignorance, without substance, like flowers in the sky, dreamlike and not real, then one should turn away from all illusory and false transformations, dissolve the existent back into emptiness, trace back to the root and exhaust the source: the ten thousand dharmas are all one substance (the true reality of all dharmas), all returning to nothing (all returning to the true and pure).

[Flowers in the sky] That is, flowers in empty space. (‘Hua’ was anciently the same as ‘flower.’) One with diseased eyes falsely sees flowers in space. Space originally has no flowers; they are only what the diseased eyes see. This is used to illustrate that the marks grasped at by the false mind are illusions. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Falsely taking the four great elements as one's own body, and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the marks of one's own mind — like a diseased eye seeing flowers in space, and a second moon.”
The Transmission of the Lamp says:
“One film over the eye, and flowers fall wildly in space.”
[No nature] Nature means substance; all dharmas have no substantial body, and this is called having no nature. The Lotus Sūtra says:
“One knows that all dharmas are ever without nature.”
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“All illusions are without nature.”

[Dissolving the existent back into emptiness] To return the illusory marks of false existence to the originally empty and nonexistent true reality. [The ten thousand dharmas are one substance] This one substance is the true reality of all dharmas. The Sūtra of the Buddha's Treasury says:
“What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.”
The Lotus Sūtra says:
“The bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as true reality, not inverted, not moving, not retreating, not turning.”

[Relying on the essence of original enlightenment, one gives rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment, turns the light back against the stream upon the self-nature's essence, clear, still, and unmoving. At the place where a thought arises, one fixes the gaze and looks steadily, observing its arising and ceasing, examining its movement and stillness. Not a single thought arising is itself the unborn. It is like watching clear water and observing where the waves arise; like watching empty space and observing where the wind stirs; like a cat watching for a mouse. The whole of one's spirit is concentrated here, the mind gathered to one point. Not for a single instant does one relax.]

Relying on the mind-essence of original enlightenment, one gives rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment and turns the light back against the stream upon this clear, still, unmoving essence of self-nature. At the place where a thought arises, one fixes the gaze and looks steadily, observing its arising and ceasing, examining its movement and stillness. (To turn back and look within, watching where thoughts arise, is like a pearl emitting light that shines back upon the pearl itself.) Not a single thought arising is itself the unborn. It is like watching clear water and observing where the waves arise; like watching empty space and observing where the wind stirs; like a cat watching for a mouse, guarding the mouth of its hole. The whole of one's spirit is concentrated here, the mind gathered to one point. Not for a single instant does one relax.

[Original enlightenment, initial enlightenment] The mind-essence (the self-nature) of all sentient beings is inherently endowed with the virtue of perfect and complete awakening; this is called original enlightenment. Yet this mind-essence of original enlightenment has, since beginningless time, been covered by ignorance and affliction and lies hidden to this day; once, by the power of cultivation, the wisdom of awakening first appears, and this is called initial enlightenment. Original enlightenment is like the full moon, initial enlightenment like the new moon: though their essence is one, what they manifest differs. The Awakening of Faith says:
“The meaning of initial enlightenment: it is because of original enlightenment that there is non-enlightenment; and it is because of non-enlightenment that initial enlightenment is spoken of.”
It also says:

“The essence of mind is free from thought; being free from the marks of thought, it is equal to the realm of empty space and pervades everywhere. The one mark of the dharma-realm is the Tathāgata's universally equal dharma-body; with reference to this dharma-body it is called original enlightenment.”
The Sūtra of the Humane King says:
“The purity of self-nature is called the nature of original enlightenment; it is the omniscience of all the Buddhas.”
[To peer (
qū

)] To narrow the eyes to a slit and look closely. [Relying on the essence of original enlightenment, giving rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment, turning the light back against the stream, clear, still, and unmoving — the essence of self-nature] To feel the noumenon (the self-nature) and contemplate the mind is like watching still, unmoving water and perceiving where the waves arise.

The method of ‘watching where thoughts arise’ described here is this: in a state of no-thought, watch where thoughts arise, investigating just before a single thought has sprouted. Hence the words, ‘It is like watching clear water and observing where the waves arise.’ Therefore one who undertakes this practice should already have a foundation in briefly keeping not a single thought arising.

The essential point in practice: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, do not let false thoughts continue and become discursive thinking — ‘when a thought arises, be aware at once; being aware, it is gone.’

[Original enlightenment, initial enlightenment, ultimate enlightenment] Original enlightenment is the pure mind-essence inherently possessed by all sentient beings; initial enlightenment is the mind-essence that, after original enlightenment has been obscured by ignorance, begins to gradually eliminate ignorance and gradually still the false mind; ultimate enlightenment is the mind-essence of final, thorough awakening — that is, the mind-essence of a Buddha.

[In the supreme meaning, all is originally pure — ask, where does it come from? Resolve to see it through till the truth stands clear. Hold tight, do not scatter; whoever comes, cut it down; any false thought, with one squeeze is shattered, its traces erased, its tracks hidden, melting like ice on the spot.]

In the supreme meaning (the true reality of all dharmas) there is originally not a single thing; if a false thought arises, ask at once where it comes from. Resolve to see it through until the truth stands clear. Gather your mental strength and press the inquiry hard; whether a thought is good or bad, whoever comes, cut it down. Any false thought, squeezed in this way (asking where it comes from), is shattered, so that it melts away completely without a trace.
[The supreme meaning] The highest and unsurpassed principle — that is, the true reality of all dharmas. The Sūtra of the Buddha's Treasury says:
“What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:

“All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is called the real, is called true reality, is called the dharma-realm, is called ultimate wisdom, is called the supreme truth, is called supreme emptiness.”
[Qu] He, it. [Za (zā)] To press and squeeze. [Hidden tracks] To vanish without a trace.
Master Hanshan said:

“Right at the place where such thoughts arise, press the pursuit straight on: here in me there was originally no such thing — ask, where does it come from? What after all is it? Resolve to see where it ends up. Squeezed on in this way, it will make gods and ghosts weep, its traces erased, its tracks hidden. Drive it out and kill it off, leaving not a thread behind. Strive in this way, and you will naturally see good news.”
(Dream Roamings
Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)
Master Hanshan also said:

“Simply in the midst of daily affairs, plant your feet firmly where mind and thoughts have not yet stirred, and turn back to look within. At the place where a thought arises, immediately pursue and examine this one thought: from where does it arise? When you pursue it to the place where the thought arises and find that it was originally unborn, then all deluded thoughts and emotional cares melt like ice on the spot. What you must guard against is lacking fierce courage, being unable to seize the throat of it, and, unaware, letting it continue — then you drift on and do not return.”
(Dream Roamings
Instructions to Minister Xiao Xuanpu)

Translation: Simply in the midst of daily life, plant your feet firmly where mind and thoughts have not yet stirred, and turn back to look within. Whenever a thought arises, immediately pursue and examine this one thought: from where does it arise? When you pursue it to the place where the thought arises and find that it was originally unborn, then all deluded thoughts and emotional cares melt like ice on the spot. What you must guard against (what you fear) is lacking fierce courage, being unable to seize the throat of it (the vital point — the place where a thought arises), losing awareness and letting false thoughts continue, so that you sink into delusion and cannot pull yourself free.
[One thought, ten thousand years]
A single thought-moment of mind encompasses ten thousand years of time without remainder.
As used for practice in the Chan school, it means: to maintain this one right mindfulness forever. For example, Mr. Liu Zhuyuan says in Essentials of the Buddha Dharma:
“Bodhidharma's three phrases
(‘Externally put to rest all conditions; inwardly the mind has no gasping; the mind is like a wall’)

, sum up everything. The Sixth Patriarch's ‘not thinking of good, not thinking of evil’ is precisely ‘externally putting to rest all conditions.’ ‘Just at such a time’ is precisely ‘inwardly the mind has no gasping.’ The words differ — how could the meaning be two? When you reach ‘just at such a time,’ there is only one unmoving flavor; practice on as one thought for ten thousand years — what dharma is there besides?”
(See, for details,
The Essential Mind of Baiyun
[Past and future cut off, the path of mind and thought extinguished,
one thought for ten thousand years, forever aware and illuminating —

clear and still, without delusion or dullness; bright and distinct, with essence and function. Striving without slackening, on until the unborn; when the melon is ripe, the stem falls — one knows for oneself whether it is cool or warm.]

Past and future cut off, the path of mind and thought extinguished, one constantly keeps watching where thoughts arise (one thought for ten thousand years), forever aware and illuminating. Clear and still, without delusion or dullness; utterly distinct (bright and clear), possessing the essence of empty stillness and the function of numinous knowing (essence and function). Striving in this way without slackening, on until the unborn (when the illuminating and the illuminated are both dissolved), when the melon is ripe the stem falls (when practice settles into one piece) — (as one who drinks water) one knows for oneself whether it is cool or warm.

[Past and future] The past bound means the past, the future bound means the future. Jingying's Commentary says: “Conditioned dharmas arise one after another, in succession. What precedes is the past bound; what follows is the future bound.” [Past and future cut off] Neither a preceding thought nor a following thought — that is, the state in which not a single thought arises. The Record of the Mirror of the Source:

“Thus the Notes on the Essentials of Mind say: if not a single thought arises, then past and future are cut off. The illuminating essence stands alone; things and self are both thus; one goes straight to the source of mind.”
The Preface to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan says:
“Hearing once, one awakens to a thousand things and attains the great dhāraṇī; not a single thought arises, and past and future are cut off.”

[The path of mind and thought extinguished] Here it means: the path of mind and thought is severed; mind and thoughts no longer stir. (Note: ordinarily, ‘the path of words is cut off, the place of mind and thought is extinguished’ means that the Tathāgata's true meaning of true emptiness and wondrous existence cannot be explained in words, nor can it be conjectured by thought. The Sūtra of the Flower in the Hand Spoken by the Buddha says:

“Worldly and world-transcending dharmas are without verbal explanation: the path of words is cut off, the place of mind and thought is extinguished. Therefore the Tathāgata, though he speaks, is unattached, and does not definitively discriminate the mark of the eye.”
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of the Humane King Who Protects the Country says:

“Not a mark, nor no mark; neither grasping nor abandoning; neither great nor small; neither seen nor heard nor sensed nor known; the place of mind and thought is extinguished, the path of words is cut off; one with the true bound, equal to the dharma-nature — by this mark do I contemplate the Tathāgata.”
) [Clear] The spirit is awake, not dull. [Still] Not a single thought arises. [Practice settles into one piece] Becoming one continuous whole, movement and stillness are one suchness.

[This is identical to turning back to contemplate one's own mind, and to turning hearing back to the self-nature. It is also the same as investigating ‘who is it?’, and it is the perfect illumination, the pure mark of enlightenment. It is the clear penetration of the original face, the wondrous nature of true suchness. It is the all-pervading contemplation of the one substance of the ten thousand dharmas, the nature of equality.]

This (watching where thoughts arise) is identical to turning back to contemplate one's own mind (the method of contemplating the mind), and to turning hearing back to the self-nature (the method of perfect penetration through the ear-faculty); it is also identical to investigating ‘who is reciting the Buddha's name,’ and it is the perfect illumination and pure mark of enlightenment in the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment; it is the clear penetration of the original face, the wondrous nature of true suchness; it is the all-pervading contemplation of the one substance and equal nature of the ten thousand dharmas.
[It is the perfect illumination, the pure mark of enlightenment] The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All Tathāgatas, in their original causal ground of arising, rely on the perfect illumination of the pure mark of enlightenment, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha way.”

[The essence of true suchness is the principle of thusness; the wondrous function of contemplation is the wisdom of thusness. Relying on the principle of thusness, one gives rise to the wisdom of thusness; with the wisdom of thusness, one illuminates the principle of thusness. The preceding thought has ceased, the following thought has not arisen; in between, utterly alone. The wisdom that contemplates contemplates this original nature, the state without thought. The utterly still thought illuminates the utterly still essence. Pressed to the utmost point, when stillness is complete, light penetrates. Still and yet illuminating, it sends forth its original bright radiance. This is freedom from thought, and then perfect illumination; it is the straightforward mind, right mindfulness of true suchness.]

The essence of true suchness is the principle of thusness; the wondrous function of contemplation is the wisdom of thusness. Relying on the principle of thusness, one gives rise to the wisdom of thusness; with the wisdom of thusness, one shines back upon the principle of thusness. The preceding thought has ceased, the following thought has not arisen; the solitary state in between, utterly alone, in which not a single thought arises, is precisely the wisdom that contemplates contemplating this original nature, the state without thought. The utterly still thought (the knowing of empty stillness) illuminates the utterly still essence. Pressed to the utmost point, when stillness is complete, light penetrates. Still and yet illuminating, it sends forth the radiance of original brightness. This is freedom from thought and then perfect illumination; it is the straightforward mind rightly mindful of true suchness.

[The essence of true suchness is the principle of thusness; the wondrous function of contemplation is the wisdom of thusness] Principle is the essence of wisdom; wisdom is the function of principle. Principle and wisdom are non-dual, essence and function are one suchness — hence the name ‘thus.’

[When the mind runs after outer objects, gather it back and make it return. When a thought arises, be aware at once; being aware, it is gone — and this very aware mind is called contemplation. Though the aware mind arises, there is no mark of awareness. What is called awareness means that the mind is free from thought. Thought after thought one is mindful of awareness, thought after thought one pursues awareness, thought after thought is awareness. Awareness and thought are both empty; aware and yet constantly illuminating, illuminating and yet constantly aware. The mirror illustrates the essence; the mirror's light illustrates the wisdom. From the mirror the light arises, and shines back upon the mirror's essence. Mirror and light are non-dual; principle and wisdom are one suchness; the essence is the function, and the function is the essence.]

When the mind runs after outer objects, gather it back and make it return. When a thought arises, be aware at once; being aware, it is gone — such an aware mind is called contemplation. Though the aware mind arises, there is no mark of awareness. What is called awareness means that the mind-essence is free from thought. Thought after thought one is mindful of awareness, thought after thought one pursues awareness, thought after thought is awareness. Awareness and thought are both empty; aware and yet constantly illuminating, illuminating and yet constantly aware. The mirror illustrates the essence (the noumenon); the mirror's light illustrates the wisdom (the knowing of empty stillness). From the mirror the light arises (from the noumenon arises the knowing of empty stillness), and shines back upon the mirror's essence (with the knowing of empty stillness one shines back upon the noumenon). Mirror and light are non-dual; principle and wisdom are one suchness; the essence is the function, and the function is the essence.
[Again, it is like a dark
(an archaic variant of ‘dark’)

room: darkness has no nature of its own; once the lamp is lit, the mark of darkness at once ceases. When true wisdom (the lamp's light) shines, where is ignorance (the mark of darkness)? The whole is precisely the great treasury of bright light. Just at such a time, wisdom and principle are both dissolved. The lone moon, round and bright; the clear sky, alone and luminous; body and mind drop away, and the light of wisdom suddenly blazes forth, and one attains immeasurable ease and freedom. This is the state when practice first gains power; one must not rejoice over it.]

Again, as in a dark room: darkness is not permanent; as soon as the lamp is lit, the mark of darkness at once ceases. When true wisdom (the lamp's light) shines, where is ignorance (the mark of darkness)? The whole is precisely the great treasury of bright light. Just at such a time, wisdom and principle are both dissolved. The lone moon, round and bright; the clear sky, alone and luminous; body and mind drop away, and the light of wisdom suddenly blazes forth, and one attains immeasurable ease and freedom. This is the state when practice first gains power; one must not rejoice and take it for the ultimate.

[To establish wisdom and establish an object, to have illumination and awareness, is the initial expedient. It still belongs to the consciousness of emotion, is likewise a flower in the sky, and is called an obstruction. With great rest and great letting go, one dispels them layer by layer, until object and wisdom are one suchness, and the one mind is perfectly bright. The illumination and that which illuminates are simultaneously extinguished; knowing without knowing, knowing yet not knowing. When the time comes, the bottom of the bucket falls out of itself.

To establish the wisdom that illuminates and the object illuminated, to have illumination and awareness — this is the initial expedient. It still belongs to the consciousness of emotion, is likewise a flower in the sky, and is entirely an obstruction. Therefore one should further rest greatly and let go greatly, dispelling them layer by layer, until object and wisdom are one suchness and the one mind is perfectly bright. The illuminating and the illuminated are simultaneously extinguished; knowing without knowing, knowing yet not knowing. When the time comes, the bottom of the black-lacquer bucket falls out of itself.

[The bottom of the bucket falls out of itself] Sentient beings' ignorance through vast kalpas, their accumulated habits glued fast, is just like a bucket that has held lacquer (a black-lacquer bucket), pitch-dark and unlit. ‘Breaking the black-lacquer bucket’ or ‘the bottom of the bucket falls out’ describes the state of shattering ignorance and suddenly awakening greatly. Chan Master Wuzu said:
“Break the lacquer bucket for him.”
(Blue Cliff Record) Xuefeng told Yantou:

“I asked Deshan about the affairs of the supreme vehicle handed down from the patriarchs; Deshan struck a blow with his staff and said, ‘Speak! What is it?’ At that moment I felt as though the bottom of a bucket had fallen out.”
(See the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp
Xuefeng Yicun)

[If there is something that contemplates, one has not yet left illusion. Awareness and the object of awareness must both be empty; emptiness and the object of emptiness must both cease. When all illusions are extinguished, the true essence reveals itself. The true object is without marks; true wisdom is without knowing. Outside wisdom there is no object; outside the object there is no wisdom. There is no wisdom apart from thusness that can realize thusness; there is no thusness apart from wisdom to be realized by wisdom. Wisdom itself is the object; the object itself is wisdom. Object and wisdom are non-dual; essence and function are one suchness. Principle is nowhere not exhausted; mirroring is nowhere not complete. Numinous and undimmed, still and yet constantly illuminating. The three times are clearly seen; the ten directions are left nothing out. The true nature of true suchness illuminates and yet is constantly still, clear and boundless, pervading the dharma-realm.]

If there is something that contemplates, one has not yet left illusion. One must still make awareness and the object of awareness both empty, and emptiness and the object of emptiness both cease. When all illusions are extinguished, the true essence reveals itself. The true object is without marks; true wisdom is without knowing. Outside wisdom there is no object; outside the object there is no wisdom. There is no wisdom apart from thusness that can realize thusness; there is no thusness apart from wisdom to be realized by wisdom. Wisdom itself is the object; the object itself is wisdom. Object and wisdom are non-dual; essence and function are one suchness. Principle is nowhere not exhausted; mirroring (the wisdom of clear mirroring) is nowhere not complete. Numinous and undimmed, still and yet constantly illuminating. The three times are clearly seen; the ten directions are left nothing out. The true nature of true suchness illuminates and yet is constantly still, clear and boundless, pervading the dharma-realm.

[Thusness] The original nature of all things, the true face of dharmas — that is, the true reality of all dharmas. [The three times] Past, present, and future. [The ten directions] East, south, west, north, southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, above, and below.

blocks.text: 9. Awareness and Consciousness in Fretful Motion

inline.s: [When one first applies effort, the subject and the object are not yet forgotten, and so object and wisdom are distinguished. When contemplation is prolonged and the practice becomes pure, coarse thoughts no longer arise, the six faculties are pure, the consciousness melts like ice, and the person has nothing to rely on.]

At the beginning of practice, the contemplating and the contemplated are not yet dissolved, and so the object (the contemplated) and the wisdom (the contemplating) are distinguished. When contemplation is prolonged and the practice becomes pure, coarse thoughts no longer arise, the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) are pure, the consciousness melts like ice, and the person has nothing to rely on.
[The subject and the object are not yet forgotten] The subject and the object are not yet dissolved. Here ‘forgotten’ means abandoned.

[By clarifying the thoughts, one becomes aware of consciousness in fretful motion, coming and going in restless succession, arising and ceasing without pause. Afflictions within the mind spring up without cause. The false mind of former times was like muddy water, in which no sand or silt could be seen. Now that the water has settled, the sand and silt appear of themselves. Though the first six are pure, the manas in turn takes the seeds of habit stored since beginningless time in the essence of the eighth consciousness, turns them out, and transmits them to the sixth, the mind-consciousness, making it impure. Hence these subtle arisings and ceasings appear, not yet wholly purified. Only when the practice is in accord can one see them.]

By clarifying and stilling the thoughts, one then feels the consciousness (the sixth consciousness) surging and fretting, coming and going in restless succession, arising and ceasing without pause. Afflictions within the mind spring up without cause. This is because the false mind of former times was like muddy water, in which no sand or silt could be seen. Now that the muddy water has settled clear, the sand and silt appear of themselves (an illustration of awareness and consciousness in fretful motion). Though the first six consciousnesses are pure and outer objects do not enter, the manas (the seventh consciousness) in turn takes the seeds of habit from beginningless kalpas stored in the essence of the ālaya-consciousness (the eighth consciousness), turns them out, and transmits them to the sixth consciousness (the mind-consciousness), so that it cannot be pure; hence these subtle arisings and ceasings appear, not yet wholly purified. It is precisely because one has the initial practice of clarifying and stilling the thoughts that one can perceive the subtle fretting of consciousness (so awareness and consciousness in fretful motion is not a retreat in practice, but a new pass to be crossed on the way forward).

[The first six consciousnesses] Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, sensing, and thinking that arise when the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) meet the six dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). Because they are the first six of the eight consciousnesses, they are often called ‘the first six consciousnesses.’ [The six faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye is the faculty of sight, the ear the faculty of hearing, the nose the faculty of smell, the tongue the faculty of taste, the body the faculty of touch, and the mind (the manas) the faculty of thought and deliberation (see, for details,
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
). [Pass (
ài
)] A strategic and dangerous checkpoint.

Therefore, when afflictions churn within the mind, one must be calm and patient and must not panic; this is precisely the critical moment when, the willows dark and the flowers bright, another village comes into view. One should at once rouse one's spirits and press forward with all one's might, as the text below says: ‘Examine closely within and investigate — who is it that is aware and illuminating?’ Working on in this fine and continuous way, once the hard pass is broken, the finest scenery lies before one's eyes.
Remember: whenever irritation flares up, that is a good opportunity to advance in practice! Make good use of it.
Concerning this pass in practice, Master Hanshan gave this instruction:

“And when practice reaches the point of gaining power, outer objects do not enter, and only afflictions within the mind spring up on every side without cause. Or desires flare up, or the mind gives rise to vexation, or all kinds of obstructions arise, until the mind is weary and the strength exhausted, and there is nothing to be done. These are the seeds of habit from measureless kalpas stored within the eighth consciousness; today, pressed hard by practice, they all come forth. Here it is most important to be clear: first one must see through them and pass beyond them; by no means be enveloped by them, by no means be toyed with by them, by no means take them as real things. Simply rouse your spirits, rouse your courage, and take up your original huatou. Right at the place where such thoughts arise, press the pursuit straight on: here in me there was originally no such thing — ask, where does it come from? What after all is it? Resolve to see where it ends up. Squeezed on in this way, it will make gods and ghosts weep, its traces erased, its tracks hidden. Drive it out and kill it off, leaving not a thread behind. Strive in this way, and you will naturally see good news. If one thought is squeezed through, then all false thoughts fall away at once, like the shadow of a sky-flower dropping, like the waves of a mirage settling clear. After passing this once, one attains immeasurable ease and immeasurable freedom. This is where the beginner gains power; it is no mystery. And when ease and freedom come, one must not give rise to a mind of joy. If one gives rise to a mind of joy, the demon of joy attaches to the mind, and there is one more obstruction.”
(Dream Roamings
Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)

Translation: If practice reaches the point of gaining power, outer objects do not enter, and only afflictions within the mind suddenly spring up on every side for no reason. Or desires flare up, or the mind gives rise to vexation, or all kinds of obstructions arise, until the mind is weary and the strength exhausted, and there is nothing to be done. These are the seeds of habit from measureless kalpas stored within the ālaya-consciousness; today, pressed hard by practice, they all come forth. This is the most critical juncture; you must be clear about it in your own mind. First you must see through them and pass beyond them; by no means be enveloped by them, by no means be toyed with by them, by no means take them as real things. Simply rouse your spirits, rouse your courage, and take up your original huatou. If desires and afflictions still hover and will not leave, then right at the place where these thoughts arise, press the pursuit straight on: here in me there was originally no such thing — ask, where does it come from? What after all is it? Resolve to see where it ends up. Squeezed on in this way, it will make gods and ghosts weep, its traces erased, its tracks hidden. Drive it out and kill it off, leaving not a thread behind. Strive in this way, and you will naturally see good news. If one thought is squeezed through, then all false thoughts fall away at once, like the shadow of a sky-flower fading, like the waves of a mirage settling clear. Having passed this one pass, one attains immeasurable ease and immeasurable freedom. This is where the beginner gains power; it must not be regarded as something mysterious. As for ease and freedom, again one must not give rise to a mind of joy. If one gives rise to a mind of joy, the demon of joy attaches to the mind, and there is one more obstruction.

[Flowers in the sky] One with diseased eyes sees flowers in space; space originally has no flowers — they are only the false seeing of diseased eyes. This uses flowers in the sky as a simile for illusions. [Mirage] A kind of vapor produced under the blazing sun that looks like water from afar; the thirsty deer longs to drink but can never obtain it — used as a simile for illusions, and one of the ten similes of the Mahāyāna. [Beginner's mind] One who has just aroused the mind to learn the Buddha's teaching.

blocks.text: 10. Who Is It That Is Aware and Illuminating?

inline.s: [When this state appears before you, press forward with all your might. Rouse your spirits, summon courage and fierceness, and do not relax. From the top of a hundred-foot pole, step on to the utmost point; examine closely within and investigate: who is it that is aware and illuminating? With this markless doubt, press hard and squeeze hard.]

When this state of awareness and consciousness in fretful motion appears before you, you should press forward with all your might. Rouse your spirits, summon courage and fierceness, and do not relax. From the top of a hundred-foot pole, step on further to the utmost point; examine closely and investigate within: who is it that is aware and illuminating? With this markless doubt, press hard and squeeze hard.
The Chan Master Daoyuan
's verse says
“He who at the hundred-foot pole's top stands still,
having already brought all back to nothing
), though he has entered, has not yet reached the real; from the hundred-foot pole he still must climb,
personally realizing the original nature
, and the worlds in all ten directions are his whole body.”
(Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
